passage:
Saturday, late. Third time this month something has gone missing from my shelf: first a charger, then some cash from my envelope, now my good headphones. My stomach has been in a knot all evening.

Madhav is the obvious one. He's the only other person with a key, and he's been strangely cheerful. I typed a message to the whole floor and deleted it. I have no proof. Anyone could walk in when the door isn't latched, and I forgot the latch twice last week.

So tomorrow I'll write down what went missing and when, keep the latch on, and ask Madhav plainly whether he's seen or borrowed anything. If it keeps happening I'll take my list to the warden. I won't accuse him without something solid.

Darshan

qa.q: What has gone missing from Darshan's shelf this month?
qa.a: A charger, some cash from the envelope and the good headphones.

qa.q: Why did Darshan delete the message meant for the whole floor?
qa.a: Darshan has no proof and does not want to accuse Madhav unfairly, since anyone could walk in when the door isn't latched.

qa.q: What plan does Darshan make for tomorrow?
qa.a: Write down what went missing and when, keep the latch on, ask Madhav plainly, and go to the warden with the list if it continues.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel if Darshan had accused him in front of the floor without evidence?
qa.a: If he is innocent, probably hurt and defensive, and the friendship would take damage that is hard to undo.

grounding: Darshan's things and money go missing; Darshan gathers facts, plans to talk to the roommate and involve the warden, and refuses to accuse without evidence.

passage:
Warden's note, Block B, 9 September
Harish came to my office this morning. Over three weeks, 1,200 rupees and a power bank had gone missing from his room. He said the whole floor assumed it was his roommate, because the roommate "is always short of money". But Harish had not accused him. He had written down the dates each thing went missing and noticed they matched days when the room had been left unlocked while both of them were in class.
He looked tired and uneasy. "I don't want to ruin someone's name on a guess," he said.
I thanked him for bringing facts, not rumours. We checked the entry register together. I have asked for locks on every room, and at tonight's floor meeting I will remind everyone not to spread accusations. Harish will talk to his roommate himself this evening, only to share what we found.
Kavitha, warden

qa.q: What had gone missing from Harish's room?
qa.a: 1,200 rupees and a power bank, over three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Harish avoid accusing his roommate?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and wanted to be fair, not wishing to ruin someone's name on a guess.

qa.q: What was done instead of accusing anyone?
qa.a: Harish logged the dates, the warden checked the entry register with him, arranged locks on every room, and planned to tell the floor to stop spreading accusations.

qa.q: What is it like for the roommate when the whole floor assumes he stole?
qa.a: Unfair and isolating: he is suspected only because he is short of money, without any proof.

grounding: Shows things going missing in a shared room, gathering facts and involving the warden rather than accusing without evidence.

passage:
Thursday
2,000 gone from my drawer. The envelope for next month's fees, just empty. My first thought was Ritu. She's been talking about wanting new shoes. I had the message typed in our flat group: "Whoever took my money, just return it." Everyone would know who I meant.
I didn't send it. I don't actually know anything. So I wrote down what I do know: the envelope was full on Sunday. The flat door was open on Tuesday afternoon when the plumber came. I was in college; so was Ritu, I checked her timetable.
Tonight I told Ritu calmly, not accusing. She went pale, then said, "I swear I didn't. Let's tell Mrs. D'Souza." We called the landlady together. She's putting a proper lock on the main door and will look into Tuesday. The money might never come back. But I still have a flatmate.
— Irawati

qa.q: How much money went missing from Irawati's drawer?
qa.a: 2,000, the envelope for next month's fees.

qa.q: What did Irawati feel on finding the envelope empty?
qa.a: Shocked and suspicious, quick to blame Ritu and tempted to post an accusation in the group.

qa.q: What did Irawati do instead of accusing Ritu?
qa.a: Wrote down the facts, spoke to Ritu calmly, and called the landlady together with her to fix the lock and look into Tuesday.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt if the group message had been sent?
qa.a: Humiliated and wrongly accused in front of everyone, which could have ended their trust.

grounding: Illustrates money going missing and the choice to gather facts, talk calmly and involve the landlady rather than accuse without evidence.
